title: Old-Time Rhubarb Forcing
subtitle: Fresh Stalks in Midwinter
items: Pack in soil in a dark cellar
intro: Farm families once forced rhubarb in the cellar to get a fresh 'fruit' in the dead of winter, a method described in old USDA Farmers' Bulletins. Frozen crowns brought into a dark, cool cellar send up tender pink stalks weeks before spring. Here is the old method in our own words.
desc: Old-time rhubarb forcing: dig mature crowns, let them freeze, then pack them in soil in a dark 50-60°F cellar and harvest tender pink stalks in midwinter. A forgotten homestead trick for fresh rhubarb in January. Full list on the blog.

title: Winter Sowing in Milk Jugs
subtitle: Start Seeds Outdoors Now
items: Cut jug around, leave a hinge
Poke drain holes in the bottom
Tape shut, leave the cap off
Open lids on warm spring days
intro: Winter sowing turns empty milk jugs into tiny greenhouses. Seeds of cold-hardy crops like kale, spinach, lettuce and onions sit outdoors all winter, then sprout on their own schedule in spring, with no grow lights and no hardening off.
desc: Winter sowing in milk jugs for beginners: cut and hinge the jug, add drainage holes and moist potting mix, sow cold-hardy vegetables like kale, spinach and lettuce, then leave it outside all winter. Easy seed starting with no grow lights. Full list on the blog.

title: Build a Lasagna Bed This Winter
subtitle: No-Dig Bed, Ready by Spring
items: Plant in spring as it settles
desc: Build a lasagna garden bed this winter with no digging: lay wet cardboard over the grass, stack layers of leaves, straw, kitchen scraps and manure 18-24 inches high, and top with compost. It settles into rich soil by spring planting. See the raised bed and compost basics. (Contains affiliate links.)

title: How to Pressure Can Turkey
subtitle: Shelf-Stable Meat, USDA Way
intro: Turkey can be home canned the same way as chicken and other poultry, but only in a pressure canner. These steps follow the hot-pack poultry directions in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, rewritten in our own words. Always check the pressure table for your altitude and gauge type.
desc: How to pressure can turkey meat safely: precook about two-thirds done, hot pack with broth, leave 1 1/4 inch headspace and process boned pints 75 minutes or quarts 90 minutes at 10 lb weighted gauge, adjusted for altitude. USDA-tested poultry method. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Dry Cranberries
subtitle: Sweet-Tart Snack That Keeps
items: Drain and pat the berries dry
Spread in one layer on trays
intro: Fresh cranberries are in every store this week, and drying a few bags gives you a sweet-tart snack for trail mix, oatmeal and baking all winter. The trick is cracking the tough skins first so moisture can escape.
desc: How to dry fresh cranberries at home: crack the skins in boiling water, sweeten lightly, dry in one layer at 135-140°F until leathery, then condition and store airtight. Homemade dried cranberries for baking and snacks. Full list on the blog.

title: Sharpen a Knife on a Whetstone
subtitle: A Skill Every Kitchen Needs
items: Sweep heel to tip, edge first
Raise a burr, then flip sides
intro: A sharp knife is safer than a dull one because it cuts where you aim instead of slipping. Learning to sharpen on a whetstone is a small self-sufficiency skill that keeps kitchen, garden and butchering knives working for decades.
desc: How to sharpen a knife on a whetstone: soak the stone, start coarse, hold a steady 15-20 degree angle, raise a burr on each side and finish on the fine grit. A simple self-sufficiency skill for kitchen and homestead knives. Full list on the blog.
